subject: Banking
title: Printing Money
description: Learn Printing Money in one minute.

hook.text: Central banks create money digitally. The Fed added $4.8 trillion during COVID by typing numbers into a computer.

buildup.text: When the Fed buys bonds, it credits the seller's bank account with new money.

discovery.text: This is called quantitative easing. The Fed doesn't print paper bills. It creates digital reserves that banks can lend.

twist.text: Money creation doesn't automatically cause inflation. If banks don't lend the new reserves, prices don't rise.

climax.text: Central banks have the power to create unlimited money.

punchline.text: $4.8 trillion created digitally. Not printed — typed into existence.

quiz.question: How did the Fed create money during COVID?
options: Digitally credited bank reserves through bond purchases

details.summary: Central banks do not literally print money, but they create digital reserves by purchasing assets like government bonds. This process, known as monetization, expands the money supply and can fuel inflation if overused.
details.whyItMatters: Excessive money creation has destroyed currencies throughout history, from Weimar Germany to Zimbabwe. Understanding the mechanics and limits of money creation is essential for evaluating central bank policy.
takeaways: Central banks create money digitally by crediting commercial bank reserves
Buying government bonds is the primary mechanism for expanding money supply
Hyperinflation occurs when money creation far exceeds economic output

faq.question: How do central banks create money?
faq.answer: The central bank buys assets, typically government bonds, from commercial banks and credits their reserve accounts with new digital money. This increases the total reserves in the banking system without any physical currency being printed.

faq.question: Why doesn't money printing always cause inflation?
faq.answer: New money only causes inflation if it enters the real economy and outpaces production of goods and services. During recessions, banks may hold excess reserves rather than lending them out, limiting the inflationary impact of money creation.
